passage: Before the city had a fire ordinance of any kind, the companies that insured the warehouses along the river kept rules of their own: a brick party wall every eighty feet, no open flame above the ground floor, a clear lane left open to the water. A warehouse that ignored them paid four times the premium, and almost none did. When the council finally legislated, it set out those three requirements in nearly the same words. The statute ______ a practice the district had followed for a decade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The insurers' three rules were already being obeyed, and the council's act put those same rules, in nearly the same words, into law: *codified*. *advertised* is the live rival, since publication is part of legislating, but the warehouses did not need to be told what they were already doing to keep their premiums down, and what the statute changes is the rules' standing, not their circulation. *relaxed* is refused by "nearly the same words," which leaves the requirements where they were. *funded* would need the council to be paying for something, and no money appears anywhere in the passage.

passage: A bronze bell is brought to pitch by turning metal away from the inside of its lip. Metal can be taken off and cannot be put back, so a founder who cuts a shade too far has a bell that will never sound its note and must go back to the furnace. Every bell is therefore cast a little above the pitch it is meant to sound, and lowered to it by degrees across several days. Casting sharp is a way of making the founder's unavoidable small errors ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Cutting is one-way, so an error that overshoots destroys the bell; starting above the note means every error still leaves metal to remove, and the bell recovers: *survivable*. *rare* is the closest rival and the reading a hurried solver takes, but nothing about where the casting starts makes the founder's hand steadier — the errors are called unavoidable, and they happen just as often. *visible* would require the practice to expose errors, and it is the slow descent by degrees, not the extra thickness, that would show them. *deliberate* misdescribes them: what is deliberate is the margin, and the errors are the thing the margin is kept against.

passage: No fiber in a hemp rope runs its whole length; most are a few feet long. The ropemaker twists fibers one way into yarns, twists yarns the other way into strands, and lays the strands back the first way into the finished rope. Nothing but friction holds any of it together. Pull on the rope and every layer strains to come undone, yet no two neighboring layers strain in the same direction, so the twist of each layer ______ the one beneath it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Each layer is turned against its neighbor, so the force that would undo one is the force that winds the next harder — and with "nothing but friction" holding the fibers, winding harder is what keeps the rope whole: *tightens*. *releases* is what a reader expects from "strains to come undone" and is the trap, but a rope that released itself under load would not hold anything. *lengthens* describes what happens to a rope that unlays, which is the failure the construction prevents. *outweighs* compares magnitudes, and the passage's point is about direction: the layers are opposed, not unequal.

passage: A type designed for six-point text is not the twelve-point drawing photographed down. Its hairlines are proportionally thicker, its counters more open, its letters set further apart; shrink the large drawing instead and the page goes muddy, the fine strokes filling with ink. A punchcutter working a family across sizes therefore drew each size afresh, and the smallest of them, seen blown up on a wall, is a coarse and ungainly thing. The two sizes read as one face on the page only because the drawings behind them are ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Thicker hairlines, opener counters and wider spacing are all departures from the large drawing, and the passage says what happens when they are not made — the page goes muddy. Sameness on the page is bought with difference in the drawings: *unlike*. *reduced* names exactly the procedure the opening sentence rejects, and the muddy page is the result of it. *related* is true and too weak to explain anything: every size in a family is related, including the reduced one that fails. *paired* describes how the sizes are sold rather than how they were cut, and the passage counts more than two.

passage: An actuary's table gives, for each age, the proportion of a large cohort that will die within the year. About any one person it says nothing: no one dies by a proportion, and the table cannot name which thirty of ten thousand forty-year-olds will be among the dead. A company insuring ten thousand lives can rely on the figure; a company insuring four cannot, though the figure is the same in both cases. The table's accuracy is a property of the ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The same figure is dependable for ten thousand lives and useless for four, so what it is true of is the mass and not its members: *aggregate*. *policyholder* is the reading the passage spends three sentences refusing — "about any one person it says nothing." *forecast* would locate the accuracy in the prediction as such, which leaves unexplained why one company may rely on it and another may not. *contract* points at the legal instrument, and nothing in the passage turns on its terms; what varies between the two companies is how many lives stand behind the number.

passage: A glass vessel carried straight from the furnace to the bench cools from the outside inward. Its skin sets while the interior is still contracting, and the finished piece holds a load locked inside it that nothing on the surface shows. Annealing — keeping the glass near red heat for hours, then letting it down a little at a time — costs most of a working day. A piece that was hurried past it may stand on a shelf for a year and then come apart at a scratch a sound one would shrug off. The year on the shelf did nothing to ______ it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The load is put into the glass as it cools and is removed only by annealing, which the piece never had; a year of standing does not take any of it away, which is why the scratch is enough: *relieve*. *worsen* is the tempting alternative, since the piece does fail after the year, but the passage gives the load as fixed at the bench and the scratch as what finds it, not a year of slow addition. *advertise* would mean the shelf made the load apparent, and the passage says nothing on the surface shows it, before or after. *measure* asks what would have gauged the load, and a shelf gauges nothing.
topic_tag: annealing and locked-in stress in glass

passage: Plant an apple seed and you will get an apple tree, but not the tree the seed came from: its fruit will be its own, usually small and sour. Every tree of a named variety in every orchard is instead a cutting from one original tree, joined to a rootstock, and then a cutting from that cutting, and so on for three hundred years. The thousands of trees that carry the name are all parts of one ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Seed does not carry the variety forward; every tree of the name is cut from a cutting of a single tree, so the whole population is that one tree continued in many places: *organism*. *planting* is the near miss and would hold if the trees had gone into the ground together, whereas the passage spreads them over three hundred years and every orchard. *orchard* is a place, and the sentence's subject is trees in many places. *season* would make the name a matter of timing, and nothing in the passage dates the trees to one.

passage: A park wall of the ordinary sort would have stopped the view at the lawn's edge. The ha-ha stops the cattle and not the view. It is a ditch, its outer face revetted in stone and its inner lip flush with the grass, so that from the windows of the house the meadow runs into the lawn without a joint and the herd appears to be grazing on the lawn itself. A beast that tries the edge finds a drop of six feet. The enclosure has been ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The ditch does everything a wall did — six feet of drop, and no beast crosses — while the view from the house runs on "without a joint": the barrier is still there and cannot be seen: *hidden*. *relocated* is the strongest rival, since a ditch is not a wall, but it sits at the same edge of the same lawn, holding the same herd off it. *narrowed* would shrink the ground enclosed, and the boundary keeps its line. *strengthened* claims more holding power than the passage offers; against cattle the wall was already sufficient, and what the ha-ha adds is the sightline, not the stopping.

passage: A club player can learn twenty moves of a main line in an evening. The moves are sound; masters have tested them for a century, and against an opponent who plays the same line he will reach move twenty-one in good order and in ten minutes. But an opponent with no taste for that line has only to play a different eighth move, and the position that follows is in no book. The prepared player and the unprepared one meet it on the same terms, except that one of them has spent an evening on a sequence without its ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: What an evening of memorizing supplies is the order of the moves; what it leaves out is why each is played, which is the only thing that would have carried over once the book ran out: *rationale*. *outcome* is the live rival, but the line does have one — the passage has the prepared player reaching move twenty-one in good order — and knowing where a line ends is no help in a position that is not in it. *notation* is the form the moves were learned in and is plainly present. *opponents* would make the missing thing a person, and the sequence is not short of one; an opponent is precisely what produced the difficulty.

passage: The statute forbidding servants to wear silk was enacted eleven times in ninety years, each time with heavier penalties and a longer list of named fabrics. Court rolls from the same decades record almost no prosecutions under it. Inventories of servants' goods, taken at death, list silk throughout the period and in rising quantities. Eleven enactments in ninety years are less the sign of a firm rule than of a rule that could not be ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Silk keeps appearing in the inventories and almost nobody is brought to court for it, so the rule is on the books and not in effect, and the legislature keeps returning to a prohibition it cannot make bite: *enforced*. *repealed* fits the persistence and nothing else: a rule that could not be repealed would stand unamended, and this one is rewritten every few years with new penalties. *drafted* is refuted by eleven successful enactments. *afforded* shifts the difficulty onto cost, and the only money in the passage is the servants' silk, which they evidently could afford.

passage: A shelving beach takes a wave apart: the water runs up the slope, loses its speed against the sand, and slides back with little left in it. A vertical concrete wall gives the wave nothing to run up. It meets the face, turns, and travels back out into the wave behind it, and the two together work at the sand where the wall stands. Each winter the foot of the wall sits lower and must be underpinned deeper. The scour at its base marks where the wall has ______ the force it was built to stop.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The wave is not spent against the wall; it turns, goes back seaward, and does its work on the sand at the foot instead — the same force, sent somewhere else: *redirected*. *dispersed* is what the beach does, and the passage sets the wall against the beach precisely because the wall does not do it. *multiplied* would require the wall to add energy, and the second wave was arriving anyway; what is new is where the two meet. *measured* would make the scour a gauge, but a gauge does not deepen every winter or need underpinning.

passage: Sixteenth-century singers read from partbooks: one small volume for each voice, holding that voice's line and no other, from the first piece in the book to the last. Nobody in the room held a document showing the four lines together, and the composer, having ruled a sheet and copied the parts out from it, had no reason to keep the sheet. A modern edition prints the four lines stacked and aligned bar by bar. That page is not something anyone in the room ever saw; it is the editor's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A sheet with the four lines together did exist once, in the composer's hand, and was thrown away; the editor builds that lost page again out of the parts that survive: *reconstruction*. *invention* would be right if the stacked page had never existed, and the passage takes care to say the composer ruled one. *convenience* names what the modern page is for and leaves out what it is — every edition is convenient, and only this one restores something missing. *correction* would require an error in the partbooks, and nothing in them is wrong; each holds its own line accurately.

passage: A cargo ship that has discharged everything rides high, its propeller half out of the water and its side turned to the wind like a sail. It steers badly and rolls in a way that can end a voyage. So before leaving an empty port it draws many tons of seawater into tanks low in the hull, carries the water across an ocean, and pumps it out again on arrival. On the ship's accounts that water is a cost. In the naval architect's drawings it is a ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Without the weight the propeller will not bite, the hull will not steer, and the roll "can end a voyage" — the water is what makes the passage possible at all, however it looks on a balance sheet: *necessity*. *luxury* is the reading the accounts invite and the drawings refuse: a luxury is what a ship could sail without. *hazard* inverts the case, making the remedy the danger; the danger in the passage is the empty hull. *commodity* would make the water something bought and sold, and it is drawn from the harbor for nothing and pumped back into the sea.

passage: Cookery manuals printed before the oven thermometer tell the reader to bake in a moderate oven, to beat the batter until it is right, to take butter the size of a walnut. Modern readers call such directions vague. They were written for women who had stood at ranges of the same kind since childhood, who could hold a hand inside an oven and count to judge its heat, and for whom a number would have said less than the walnut did. A direction written for a reader like that is not imprecise; it is ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The manuals leave out what their reader already had — a hand that could judge an oven, an eye that knew a finished batter — so the instruction is complete only when she supplies the missing part: *elliptical*. *approximate* is the strongest rival and is the charge the last sentence explicitly sets aside; it would also be false of the walnut, which the passage says told such a reader more than a number would. *careless* attributes the gaps to the writer's inattention, and they are pitched at a particular reader. *provisional* would make the directions temporary or subject to revision, and nothing in the passage suggests they were held open.

passage: A river entering a reservoir slows, and the sand and silt it has been carrying settle to the bottom. What leaves by the outlet works is clear water, and clear water has capacity to spare: it makes up its missing load from whatever lies within reach. Below such a dam the bed cuts down year after year, gravel bars vanish, and banks that stood a century slump into the channel. The reach downstream is being ______ by water that arrives carrying nothing.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The clear water takes its load out of the bed and banks and carries it away, so the reach is being worked for material the way a seam is: *mined*. *silted* is the reading a solver reaches for on seeing a dam and is the exact reverse of the case — the silt stays in the reservoir, and the water below arrives with none. *flooded* concerns how much water passes, and the passage never varies the flow; what changes is what the water carries. *graded* implies a channel being smoothed toward an even profile, whereas the passage describes a bed cutting down and banks falling in.

passage: A silversmith's own stamp says what he would like a buyer to believe. The assay office's mark says what a scraping from the piece, cupelled and weighed, was found to contain. The office neither buys nor sells plate, is paid the same fee whether the metal passes or fails, and breaks a failed piece on the spot rather than returning it to the maker. The mark is worth anything to a buyer only because the office that strikes it is ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Every fact the passage supplies is about stake: the office trades in nothing, earns the same fee either way, and gains nothing by passing a piece — it has no interest in the outcome it reports, which is what makes the mark worth more than the maker's stamp: *indifferent*. *experienced* is the live rival, and cupelling does take skill, but skill would not separate the office from the silversmith, who has plenty and whose stamp is still worthless. *ancient* rests on the age of the institution, which the passage never mentions. *local* would make proximity the guarantee, and a nearby office with a stake would be worth no more than the smith.
